clue.text: Some 22, and all other footwear

indicators.note: some of means only part of the phrase's run of letters is kept, the inner stretch

parts.note: 22-down's answer is BOOTS, making the phrase 'boots and all'

explanation.surface: A shopper wants some boots and every other kind of shoe as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes a run of letters from 'boots and all', the phrase made by putting in 22-down's answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandal is a light open shoe, so footwear other than boots fits it.

clue.text: Defence attorney likes it better if leads not followed?

indicators.note: only the leading letters are taken, and not the letters that follow them

explanation.surface: A lawyer prefers it when clues to a crime are not pursued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads' looks like detective clues; it means the first letters of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a defence that the accused was somewhere else at the time.

clue.text: Go working at the local pharmacy?

definitions.text: Go working at the local pharmacy?

parts.words: Go working at the local pharmacy?
parts.note: to go is to die, and dying while still at work is the idiom

explanation.walkthrough: Boots is the UK's best-known high-street chemist, so 'in one's Boots' is at the local pharmacy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone who dies still active, or meets a violent end, rather than in bed.

clue.text: Working party in Lisbon evacuated capital

indicators.note: in puts the working party inside the emptied city
evacuated means emptied, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: on means working, as a machine is on
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A team on duty in Lisbon empties a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evacuated' leaves LN from Lisbon, and ONDO goes 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: London is the capital city of the United Kingdom and England.

clue.text: Heralds of Cockney birth? Changing first note, do these sound lower?

indicators.note: the opening letter is the musical note B, and it is swapped for another note, C

parts.note: a true Cockney is said to be born within the sound of Bow Bells, the bells of St Mary-le-Bow in London

explanation.surface: A musing on bells announcing a Londoner's birth, and whether retuning makes them sound deeper.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow Bells are the bells of a City of London church; being born within earshot makes you a Cockney. 'Lower' is not 'deeper' but 'one that lows', a cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Bells hung on cattle ring out from animals that low, so they are heard from lowing beasts.

clue.text: Sweet logic on diet — plum duff!

indicators.note: duff is British slang for bad or broken, so the letters are faulty and remade

explanation.surface: Diet thinking applied to plum pudding is nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duff' looks like the pudding in plum duff, but is the anagram signal for LOGIC ON DIET PLUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A clootie dumpling is a Scottish fruit pudding boiled in a cloth, a dessert or sweet.

clue.text: Misinterpretation, with and without a part

parts.note: an actor between roles is said to be resting

explanation.surface: A text misread both with and without one of its sections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resting' is the theatre euphemism for an actor out of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Wresting a text means twisting its sense, so a wresting is a distortion of meaning.

clue.text: Odd pieces from Mad Max era later the preserve of the EU?

indicators.note: odd pieces means the letters are scrambled bits to be reshaped

explanation.surface: Strange bits from a dystopian film later come under European control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'preserve' is jam, not a privilege: EU rules use 'extra' for a fruit-rich grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra marmalade is a category in EU food law for marmalade with a higher fruit content, so a preserve defined by the EU.

clue.text: Probably parrot will shear mass of tissue up

indicators.note: the bird cuts into the other piece, sitting inside it
up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a tonsil is a mass of tissue in the throat
the kea is a New Zealand parrot

explanation.surface: A parrot will likely snip at some tissue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns TONSIL to LISNOT; the kea 'will shear' it, cutting in.
explanation.definitionFit: Like as not is an idiom meaning probably, more likely than not.

clue.text: 'Tired and emotional' oenophile given a little grape to classify

indicators.note: a British euphemism for drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order
only a little of the word grape is used, its first letter

explanation.surface: A tipsy wine lover is handed a grape to identify.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tired and emotional' is a British press euphemism for drunk, used as the anagram signal on OENOPHILE plus G.
explanation.definitionFit: To pigeonhole something is to put it into a category, often too neatly.

clue.text: Spot what's not worn by B-team from the East?

indicators.note: in an across clue, coming from the east means reading from right to left

parts.note: the B-team wears its own strip, not the A kit

explanation.surface: A reserve side from the East has a mark on what they are not wearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the East' turns A KIT, the first team's strip, which the B-team does not wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A tika is a coloured mark worn on the forehead by Hindus, a small spot.

clue.text: Indicate the last job typist wants boss to do today?

definitions.meaning: a ... as a verb means to point out or show

definitions.text: the last job typist wants boss to do today?
definitions.meaning: the boss must sign the post, the day's letters, before it goes out

explanation.surface: An office secretary hints that the boss's final task of the day awaits.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into SIGN POST: put a signature on the outgoing mail.
explanation.definitionFit: To signpost something is to mark or point it out clearly, which is to indicate it.

clue.text: Poor inamoratas denied special sari, without exception

indicators.note: poor shows the letters of the first word are in bad shape and must be rearranged
denied shows letters taken away, and special says the word sari is to be removed in any order

explanation.surface: Penniless lovers are refused a special sari, every last one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of SARI out of INAMORATAS ('denied special') and rearrange what is left ('Poor').
explanation.definitionFit: To a man is an idiom meaning every single one, with no one left out.

clue.text: Suffering something picked up from boulangerie?

definitions.meaning: the French for bread, what you would buy at a French bakery

explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' means bought, not heard: the French word for bread is spelt like the English one.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain is hurt or distress, the state of suffering.

clue.text: Hope to double up this tidy sum?

definitions.text: Hope to double up this tidy sum?

parts.words: Hope to double up this tidy sum?
parts.note: a bob is an old British shilling and also Bob Hope's first name, so one Bob or two makes a decent amount

explanation.walkthrough: A bob was an old British shilling; 'Hope' is the comedian Bob Hope, so doubling him gives two bobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob or two is British slang for a fair amount of money.

clue.text: Explicitly reviewed when I'm on OED shows

indicators.note: reviewed read as re-viewed backwards: the letters run the other way
shows means the answer is on display within the run of words

explanation.surface: A dictionary user's comment on what turns up when they look things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' finds ENIMONOE in 'when I'm on OED' and 'reviewed' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Eo nomine is Latin for 'by that name', used to mean expressly or explicitly.

clue.text: See 7
Bum tune broadcast after 4?

indicators.note: broadcast as in spoken over the airwaves, so the words are heard

parts.note: the Londonderry Air is the Irish tune, which comes after London, 4-down's answer

explanation.surface: A tune played on the radio after a certain item.
explanation.walkthrough: After 4, LONDON, the tune is the Londonderry Air, the melody of Danny Boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A derriere is a polite borrowing from French for the backside or bottom.

clue.text: Film director who explored how autocues might be redeployed

indicators.note: redeployed letters are put into different positions, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A director's teleprompters get moved around the set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how' is a link word: the letters of AUTOCUES 'might be redeployed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Cousteau made undersea documentary films and explored the oceans.

clue.text: Posh hotel documents delivered?

indicators.note: delivered as in spoken, a speech being delivered out loud

parts.note: writs are legal documents

explanation.surface: A smart hotel receives papers handed over by a courier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivered' looks like posting, but means spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ritz is the famous luxury hotel in London, a byword for swank.

clue.text: Catching this fish after 6 could be grave?

indicators.note: catching means hearing, catching what someone says

parts.note: a grave is a resting place; with 6-down's answer before it, the word is place

explanation.surface: Landing this fish after six o'clock could be serious.
explanation.walkthrough: After 6, WRESTING, the pair sounds like 'resting place', a grave. 'Catching' looks like fishing, but means hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaice is a European flatfish with orange spots, a common food fish.

clue.text: Could this render one, in full cry, out of bounds?

definitions.text: Could this render one, in full cry, out of bounds?

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the word for a loud call

parts.note: a roar is a cry at full volume
OB is the golf abbreviation for out of bounds

explanation.surface: Could some device stop a bellowing creature from straying where it shouldn't?
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is a kangaroo: a roo bar on the front of an Australian vehicle keeps a leaping roo off the road ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: A roo bar is a strong metal guard on a vehicle's front, built to fend off kangaroos.

clue.text: See 3
Spotted US President now doing U-turn? Not fully

parts.note: James K. Polk was the eleventh US President

indicators.note: a U-turn sends the word back the way it came
not fully means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: today means now, at the present time

explanation.surface: A sighting of a current American leader who is busy reversing policy, though only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fully' cuts TODAY to TODA; 'doing U-turn' makes it ADOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Polka-dot fabric is covered in round spots, so it is spotted.

clue.text: What braces a person supporting the Socceroos?

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits below the other one

parts.note: the Socceroos are Australia's national football team; Oz is Australia
one means a person, as in 'one should'

explanation.surface: What holds up a fan of Australian football?
explanation.walkthrough: 'braces' is not trouser straps but invigorates: seaside air is called bracing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozone is popularly the fresh sea air thought to be bracing and invigorating.

clue.text: Oil all but outer area of 17

indicators.note: everything except the outside letters, so the two end letters go

parts.note: 17-down's answer is DERRIERE, a bottom

explanation.surface: Oiling everything except the outer part of a backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 17-down is DERRIERE, which means BOTTOM; strip its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, or attar, is a fragrant essential oil pressed from rose petals.

clue.text: Knockout food shop threatening to break free of shackles

indicators.note: shackles are on the outside, so freeing the whole drops its two end letters

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a shop selling prepared food
minatory means threatening

explanation.surface: A boxer's finishing punch, while a grocer menaces to escape restraints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to break free of shackles' removes the outer D and Y from DELIMINATORY.
explanation.definitionFit: An eliminator is a knockout round or contest in which losers are put out.

clue.text: Nothing the matter? Look at horse!

parts.note: goo is sticky matter
to see is to look at
gee-gee is a childish word for a horse, GG for short

explanation.surface: Someone asks what's wrong and is told to look at the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Goose egg is American slang for zero, a score of nothing, from the shape of the numeral.

clue.text: See bolts levered out from vandalised letterboxes

indicators.note: levered out shows the second word's letters are prised away from the first
vandalised letters are smashed up and must be reassembled

explanation.surface: Bolts are prised from postboxes that someone has damaged.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove B, O, L, T, S ('levered out') from LETTERBOXES and rearrange the rest ('vandalised').
explanation.definitionFit: A see is a bishop's seat or diocese; Exeter is a cathedral city with its own bishop.
